sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in downtown Cincinnati
National Register of Historic Places listings in Cincinnati
Wikipedia GeoSearch, 2 km radius around Fountain Square

stops.name: Tyler Davidson Fountain
stops.description: The bronze Genius of Water has been the city's meeting place since 1871, and the plaza was rebuilt around her in 2006 when the fountain was shifted west off the old streetbed.

stops.name: Carew Tower
stops.description: A 49-story Art Deco tower finished in 1930 that held the title of tallest building in Cincinnati for eighty-one years.

stops.name: Ingalls Building
stops.description: Built in 1903, this 16-story block was the first reinforced concrete skyscraper anywhere, and skeptics expected it to fall down the moment the forms came off.

stops.name: Contemporary Arts Center
stops.description: Zaha Hadid's stacked-box museum opened here in 2003 and reads as a puzzle of shifted volumes from the sidewalk.

stops.name: Cincinnati City Hall
stops.description: Samuel Hannaford's 1893 Richardsonian Romanesque seat of government, in red sandstone and pink granite under a clock tower.

stops.name: Cathedral Basilica of St. Peter in Chains
stops.description: A Greek Revival cathedral finished in 1845 whose single white spire was the tallest thing on the Cincinnati skyline for decades.

stops.name: Isaac M. Wise Temple
stops.description: The 1866 Plum Street Temple, Moorish Revival with twin minarets, was the pulpit of Isaac Mayer Wise, a founder of American Reform Judaism.

stops.name: Arnold's Bar and Grill
stops.description: Cincinnati's oldest continuously operating bar, pouring since 1861 out of a pair of joined Italianate storefronts.

stops.name: Taft Museum of Art
stops.description: The oldest wooden house still standing downtown, built around 1820, now holding the art collection its last private owners gave to the city.

stops.name: National Underground Railroad Freedom Center
stops.description: Opened on the riverfront in 2004, put deliberately at the point where freedom seekers crossed the Ohio out of a slave state.

stops.name: John A. Roebling Suspension Bridge
stops.description: When it opened in 1867 this was the longest suspension bridge in the world, and Roebling carried what he learned here into the Brooklyn Bridge sixteen years later.

stops.name: Cincinnati Music Hall
stops.description: A Venetian Gothic hall of 1878 and a National Historic Landmark, designed with a concert auditorium in the middle and industrial exhibition wings on either side.

stops.name: Hamilton County Memorial Building
stops.description: Memorial Hall went up in 1908 as a Beaux-Arts tribute to county soldiers and still seats an audience next door to Music Hall.

stops.name: Washington Park
stops.description: Six acres of Over-the-Rhine green that served as Presbyterian and Episcopal burial grounds before the city bought them in the 1850s and 1860s.

stops.name: Findlay Market
stops.description: Ohio's oldest continuously operating public market and the last survivor of the nine markets that once fed the city.

note: Cincinnati had never come up; the previous six mornings ran Atlanta through Chicago alphabetically. Fifteen stops verified, all on one walkable spine from the riverfront up Vine and Elm through downtown into Over-the-Rhine. Findlay Market is the north end at roughly 1.3 miles from Fountain Square, a little past a 1-mile loop but the natural terminus of that corridor. Every street address was confirmed against the US Census geocoder, which returned ZIP 45202 for all of them. Two caveats. Findlay Market's published address is 1801 Race St while Wikipedia gives only the descriptive 'Esplanade at Elder St., between Elm and Race Sts.'; the Census geocoder has 1800 and 1802 Race St in 45202 but not 1801, so that house number comes from the market rather than from a geocoder match. The Roebling Bridge has no street address, so address and zip are null, and it closes periodically for rehabilitation (nine months in 2021 was the last one the article records), so pedestrian access is worth a check before it becomes a stop. Dropped for lack of any verifiable street address: Piatt Park, Dixie Terminal, the Homage to Cincinnatus mural, and the Lincoln statue in Lytle Park, all of which have articles and coordinates but no address in the sources swept. Also skipped Paycor Stadium and Great American Ball Park as too far from the historic core to walk to and too obvious to be interesting stops.
